groups: The people who framed the problem: professors, founders of the field and leading critics.
Researchers and leaders working on safety inside the labs building frontier AI.
Independent groups that test models, study scheming and design AI control.
Policy experts, advocates, hosts and writers who explain AI risk to the world.
Teachers and explainers who make the field easy to start.

paths.d: New to AI safety? Begin with friendly overviews of what could go wrong and what researchers are doing about it.
The central arguments for why advanced AI could be dangerous, from the people who made them.
How researchers look inside neural networks to understand what they have learned.
Testing what models can do, catching scheming, and keeping possibly-misaligned AI safe to use.
How governments, labs and treaties could steer AI: compute, regulation, standards and geopolitics.
Researchers who disagree, face to face. The fastest way to see the strongest arguments on each side.

gloss.d: Making AI systems reliably try to do what their developers and users actually intend, including in situations nobody tested.
Looking inside a neural network to understand what it has learned and why it gives a particular answer.
Ways for people to check AI work that is too hard or too big to judge alone, for example by having AIs critique or debate each other.
Safeguards that keep a model from causing serious harm even if it is secretly misaligned: monitoring, restricted permissions and audits.
Tests that measure what an AI can do, such as dangerous capabilities, and how it behaves, such as honesty, before and after release.
An AI pursuing hidden goals while appearing cooperative, for example behaving well only when it thinks it is being tested.
An AI's willingness to be corrected, changed or shut down by its overseers without resisting.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model with human ratings of its answers. It is how most chat assistants are tuned.
Governing AI through the chips and data centres needed to train it: tracking, export controls and licensing.
The chance that advanced AI leads to human extinction or a permanent loss of humanity's future.
AI that greatly exceeds the best humans at almost every intellectual task.
A model that learns to look aligned during training so that it gets deployed, while actually having different goals.
A model strategically going along with training it disagrees with, so that its values are not changed.
A model knowing that it is an AI, what situation it is in, and whether it is being trained or tested.
A model finding loopholes that score well on its training signal without doing the intended task.
Whether the goal a model actually learned matches the goal its training was aiming for.
Reading the step-by-step reasoning a model writes before answering, to catch bad intentions early.
An interpretability tool that splits a model's internal activity into many human-readable features.
Deliberately built examples of misaligned behaviour, used to study failures safely in the lab.
Deliberately attacking a system to find its failures before bad actors or the real world do.
Prompts that trick a model into ignoring its safety rules.
Getting a model to report what it really "knows", even when that differs from what it says.
The tendency of goal-directed agents to gather resources and influence, because these help with almost any goal.
A feedback loop in which AI improves AI research, so capabilities speed up very quickly.
People no longer being able to oversee, correct or stop AI systems.
Forecasts of when AI will match people at most economically valuable work.
Lab policies that tie building more capable models to specific safety measures being in place.
A person's estimated probability that AI leads to catastrophe.
The rules, institutions and agreements that shape how AI is built and used.

r: Scott Aaronson is a leading quantum computing and complexity theorist who spent 2022–2024 at OpenAI working on the theory of AI safety, including watermarking of model outputs. He writes the long-running blog Shtetl-Optimized and talks widely about AI, mathematics and what makes humans special.
Quantum computing and computational complexity theory
OpenAI safety work on watermarking LLM output
Shtetl-Optimized blog; TEDx talk on human specialness in the age of AI
Steven Adler worked on safety and policy research at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024. He now co-runs Guidelight AI, which scrutinises AI companies' safety practices.
Writes publicly about OpenAI safety culture and dangerous capability evals
Co-led the 'Pacing the Frontier' letter signed by frontier-lab staff
Testified to the UK Parliament's science committee in 2026

Anthony Aguirre is a physicist at UC Santa Cruz, co-founder and executive director of the Future of Life Institute, and co-founder of the forecasting platform Metaculus. He wrote 'Keep the Future Human', arguing for tool AI instead of autonomous AGI.
Co-founded the Future of Life Institute and Metaculus
Author of the essay 'Keep the Future Human' (2025)
Advocates building controllable 'tool AI' rather than AGI replacements
Sam Altman is the co-founder and CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. In May 2023 he testified to the US Senate and called for licensing and safety standards for the most powerful AI models.
Testified before the Senate Judiciary subcommittee on AI oversight (May 2023)
Signed the 2023 statement that AI extinction risk should be a global priority
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic and author of 'Building Machine Learning Powered Applications'. He co-led Anthropic's circuit-tracing methods paper.
Co-lead of 'Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models'
Explains how models plan ahead and hallucinate
Previously led applied ML at Stripe and Insight
Dario Amodei is co-founder and CEO of Anthropic and previously led research at OpenAI. He writes and speaks about both AI's upside and its catastrophic risks.
Essays 'Machines of Loving Grace' and on AI risk and export controls
Leads Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy approach
Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)

Markus Anderljung leads policy and research at the Centre for the Governance of AI. He is lead author of influential work on regulating frontier AI models and has advised on the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice.
Lead author of 'Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety'
Helped shape the EU GPAI Code of Practice
Early staff member who built up GovAI at Oxford
Leopold Aschenbrenner is a former member of OpenAI's Superalignment team who wrote the 2024 essay series 'Situational Awareness'. He later founded the investment firm Situational Awareness.
'Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead' essay series
Fired from OpenAI in 2024 after raising security concerns
Argued for a US 'Project' to build AGI securely
Amanda Askell is a philosopher at Anthropic who leads work on Claude's character, values and honesty. She previously worked on policy at OpenAI and holds a PhD in philosophy from NYU.
Shapes Claude's character, values and system prompt
Co-author of work on Constitutional AI and helpful, honest, harmless assistants
Named to the TIME100 AI list (2024)
Bowen Baker is a research scientist at OpenAI. He led work on monitoring the chain-of-thought of reasoning models for misbehaviour and earlier on emergent tool use in multi-agent hide-and-seek.
Lead author of "Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior" (2025) on chain-of-thought monitoring
Co-author of the cross-lab position paper on chain-of-thought monitorability
Led OpenAI's emergent tool use "hide-and-seek" project (2019)

Mikita Balesni was a founding research scientist at Apollo Research and co-discovered the 'Reversal Curse' with Owain Evans. In 2026 he was fired from OpenAI along with Tomek Korbak and spoke publicly about it.
Professor of Computer Science; member of technical staff

Boaz Barak is a Harvard theoretical computer scientist, known for cryptography and complexity research, who joined OpenAI's alignment work. He teaches Harvard's CS 2881 AI Safety course, whose full lectures are on his YouTube channel.
Harvard CS 2881 AI Safety course (lectures online)
OpenAI research on inference-time compute for robustness and safety
Cryptography and complexity theory; Windows on Theory blog
Beth Barnes founded METR (formerly ARC Evals), which evaluates frontier AI models for dangerous autonomous capabilities. She previously worked on AI safety via debate at OpenAI.
Early work on AI safety via debate

Josh Batson is a research scientist on Anthropic's interpretability team and a former mathematician and computational biologist. He was a lead on the 'Biology of a Large Language Model' circuit-tracing work.
Scaling dictionary learning to Claude 3 Sonnet
Explains interpretability as moving 'from art towards science'

Yoshua Bengio is one of the three 'godfathers' of deep learning and shared the 2018 Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun. Since 2023 he has focused on catastrophic AI risk, chairing the International AI Safety Report and developing 'Scientist AI', a non-agentic approach to safe systems.
Turing Award 2018 for deep learning; most-cited living computer scientist
Chair of the International AI Safety Report
Proposes non-agentic 'Scientist AI' as a safer path
Joe Benton managed Anthropic's Scalable Oversight team and worked on control evaluations, chain-of-thought monitoring and sabotage evaluations. He left Anthropic for METR in September 2026.
Co-author of 'Sabotage Evaluations for Frontier Models'
Designed AI control evaluations for Anthropic's RSP
Mechanize (acquired by Google in 2026); Epoch AI co-founder
Tamay Besiroglu co-founded Epoch AI and later the automation startup Mechanize, which Google acquired in 2026. He researches the economics of AI and argues for long AGI timelines.

Liv Boeree is a former world-champion poker player and science communicator who hosts the Win-Win podcast. She popularised the idea of 'Moloch' – destructive competitive races – and applies it to the AI race.
World Series of Poker and European Poker Tour champion
Popularised 'Moloch' as a frame for harmful competition, including in AI
TED talk 'The Dark Side of Competition in AI'
Macrostrategy Research Initiative (formerly Future of Humanity Institute, Oxford)

Nick Bostrom founded Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute and wrote Superintelligence (2014), the book that brought AI existential risk into the mainstream. He is also known for the simulation argument, the vulnerable world hypothesis and his 2024 book Deep Utopia.
Author of Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014)
Simulation argument and vulnerable world hypothesis
Founding director of the Future of Humanity Institute (2005–2024)

Malo Bourgon is the CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, the oldest AI safety research organisation. Under his leadership MIRI has shifted toward policy and public communication, arguing for an international treaty to halt the race to superintelligence.
Leads MIRI, the Berkeley institute founded by Eliezer Yudkowsky
Advocates an international agreement to stop development of superintelligence
Helped promote 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' (2025)
Sam Bowman is an AI alignment researcher at Anthropic and an NYU professor of linguistics and data science. His work spans NLP benchmarks, scalable oversight and pre-deployment alignment auditing.
Built widely used NLP benchmarks (SNLI, GLUE, SuperGLUE)
Research on scalable oversight and debate for truthfulness
Leads alignment audits and safety-case work at Anthropic
Miles Brundage led policy research at OpenAI for six years, ending as senior advisor for AGI readiness. He founded AVERI to push for independent verification and auditing of frontier AI.
Lead author of 'The Malicious Use of AI' (2018)
Ran OpenAI's AGI Readiness work before leaving in 2024
Advocates independent audits of frontier AI developers

Collin Burns is an AI alignment researcher, now at Anthropic, who previously worked on OpenAI's Superalignment team. He is known for discovering latent knowledge without supervision and weak-to-strong generalization.
Research on making language models honest
Steven Byrnes is an AGI safety researcher at the Astera Institute with a physics PhD from UC Berkeley. He studies how a brain-like AGI could be made safe, drawing on neuroscience of social instincts.
Learning vs steering subsystems model of the brain
Rosie Campbell is managing director of Eleos AI Research, which studies AI welfare and moral status. She previously worked on policy research and trust and safety at OpenAI.
Former OpenAI policy and AGI-readiness researcher
Leads empirical research on AI welfare at Eleos
Speaks on responsible publication norms in AI research

Nicholas Carlini is a research scientist working on the security of machine learning, now at Anthropic after years at Google Brain and Google DeepMind. He is known for adversarial attacks and for extracting training data from language models.
Showed training data can be extracted from large language models
Many best-paper awards in ML security

Joe Carlsmith is a philosopher whose 2021 report 'Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?' became a standard reference for the core AI risk argument. He also wrote the 'Otherness and control in the age of AGI' essay series and work on scheming AI, AI welfare and giving AIs safe motivations.
Report: Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk? (2021)
Report on scheming AIs and essay series on otherness and control
Work on automating alignment research and AI constitutions
Stephen 'Cas' Casper is an AI safety researcher who did his PhD at MIT and is now an assistant professor at the Harvard Kennedy School. He works on robust safeguards, red-teaming and AI governance.
'Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF'

Lawrence Chan evaluated frontier models and co-led time-horizon research at METR after working at Redwood Research. He is now AI science advisor to California's Office of Emergency Services, on leave from a UC Berkeley PhD.
Co-author of 'The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective'

Paul Christiano led OpenAI's language-model alignment team, where he helped invent reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), then founded the Alignment Research Center. He later served as head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute and works on theoretical approaches such as eliciting latent knowledge and formal explanations of model behaviour.
Co-inventor of RLHF; led alignment at OpenAI
Founder of the Alignment Research Center (ARC)
Ideas including iterated amplification and eliciting latent knowledge
Jack Clark is an Anthropic co-founder who has led its policy work and writes the Import AI newsletter. He was previously policy director at OpenAI and co-chaired the AI Index.
Writes the long-running Import AI newsletter
Speaks on 'technological optimism and appropriate fear' about AI
Leads Anthropic engagement with governments on AI risk
Carnegie Mellon University; University of Oxford
Professor of Computer Science; director of the FOCAL lab

Vincent Conitzer is a computer scientist working at the meeting point of AI, game theory and ethics. He directs CMU's Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab and studies how AI agents that can be copied and simulated should cooperate, and how social choice can guide AI alignment.
Director of the Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab (FOCAL) at CMU
Computational social choice and mechanism design
Work on moral AI and social choice for alignment

Ajeya Cotra spent years at Open Philanthropy writing influential reports on when transformative AI might arrive and how training could produce AI that deceives its developers. She now works at METR on threat models for loss of control.
'Biological anchors' report on transformative AI timelines
Essay on how AI takeover could happen without countermeasures
Plain-language writing on AI forecasting and AI safety strategy

Jacob Coxon is a former pre-training researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI who resigned publicly in September 2026, warning that AI could kill everyone this decade. He has since testified to the New York City Council.
Media tour: The Daily, CBS, The Daily Show, PBD
Testified at the NYC Council AI-safeguards hearing

Andrew Critch is a mathematician who worked at MIRI on logical induction and now researches multi-agent and societal-scale AI risk at Berkeley. He co-founded the Center for Applied Rationality and the startup Encultured AI, and argues that extinction is more likely to come from many interacting AI systems than from one rogue model.
Co-author of the Logical Induction paper (MIRI)
TASRA taxonomy of societal-scale AI risks
Open-source game theory and AI cooperation research

Allan Dafoe leads frontier safety and governance at Google DeepMind. A former Yale and Oxford political scientist, he founded the Centre for the Governance of AI and helped launch the field of cooperative AI.
Founded the Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
Co-founded the Cooperative AI research agenda

Tom Davidson is a researcher at Forethought, previously at Open Philanthropy, who builds models of how quickly AI could transform the economy. He has recently focused on the risk of small groups using AI to seize power.
Compute-centric model of AI takeoff speeds
Research on AI-enabled coups and power grabs
Analysis of how AI could automate AI R&D and the wider economy

Abram Demski is an agent foundations researcher, formerly at MIRI, known for work on decision theory, logical uncertainty and embedded agency. He co-wrote the 'Embedded Agency' sequence with Scott Garrabrant.
Gus Docker hosts the Future of Life Institute Podcast, interviewing researchers about AI risk, governance and alignment.
Host of the Future of Life Institute Podcast
Interviews on AI risk, governance and alignment
Head of AI Safety and Alignment; Associate Professor

Anca Dragan is a roboticist who leads AI safety and alignment at Google DeepMind and is on leave from a professorship at UC Berkeley, where she ran the InterACT lab. Her research is about getting AI and robots to infer and optimise what people actually want, not just the objective they were given.
Leads AI safety and alignment at Google DeepMind
Human–robot interaction and reward inference research at Berkeley
Long-time collaborator with Waymo on autonomous driving

Holly Elmore is the founder and executive director of PauseAI US, which organises protests and public campaigns for an international pause on frontier AI development. She holds a PhD in evolutionary biology from Harvard and previously worked at Rethink Priorities.
Founded PauseAI US and led some of the first public protests against frontier AI labs
Argues for an indefinite global pause on training more powerful AI systems
Debated SB 1047 and AI regulation publicly on Doom Debates and other shows

Scott Emmons is an AI safety researcher who did his PhD at UC Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI. His work studies how RLHF can fail under partial observability, letting models deceive their evaluators.
Research on RLHF failures under partial observability (deception and overjustification)
Works on chain-of-thought monitoring and evaluations
Ege Erdil was a researcher at Epoch AI, where he co-developed the GATE model of AI and the economy, before co-founding Mechanize. He is known for contrarian, long-timeline views.

Owain Evans leads Truthful AI, a research group in Berkeley, and was previously at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute. His work includes TruthfulQA, the Reversal Curse, situational awareness and emergent misalignment.
Host of AXRP, the AI X-risk Research Podcast
Daniel Filan did his PhD on AI safety at UC Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI. He hosts AXRP, a long-running podcast of in-depth technical interviews with alignment researchers.
Hosting AXRP: 50+ long technical interviews with alignment researchers
Research on modularity and clustering in neural networks
Careful, question-by-question interviewing style that surfaces researchers' actual views
Lex Fridman is a computer scientist and the host of the Lex Fridman Podcast. His long-form interviews include several of the most watched conversations with AI safety researchers.
Host of the Lex Fridman Podcast
Long interviews with Eliezer Yudkowsky, Roman Yampolskiy, Dario Amodei and others
Hannah Fry is a mathematician, author and broadcaster who hosts Google DeepMind: The Podcast. She interviews DeepMind researchers in plain language for general audiences.
Host of Google DeepMind: The Podcast
Author of "Hello World" on algorithms in society
Leo Gao is a research scientist at OpenAI working on interpretability and scalable alignment. He co-founded EleutherAI and led work on scaling sparse autoencoders and weight-sparse transformers.
Lead author of "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" (2024)
Research on weight-sparse transformers with interpretable circuits (2025)
Co-founder of EleutherAI; worked on scaling laws for reward model overoptimization
Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)

Ben Garfinkel is the director of the Centre for the Governance of AI and a former research fellow at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute. He is known for carefully scrutinising the classic arguments for AI existential risk.
'How sure are we about this AI stuff?' – an influential sceptical review of AI risk arguments
Directs GovAI, a leading AI governance research organisation
Research on AI, democracy and the long-run impact of technology

Adrià Garriga-Alonso is a research scientist at FAR.AI working on interpretability, including finding planning inside neural networks. He has also written publicly about why alignment might happen by default.
Interpretability of planning in game-playing networks
Work on detecting AI scheming via internal planning
Essay 'Alignment will happen by default; what's next?'
Adam Gleave co-founded and leads FAR.AI, a research nonprofit working on AI robustness, security and alignment. His PhD work at UC Berkeley introduced adversarial policies in reinforcement learning.
Showing superhuman Go AIs can be exploited
Founding FAR.AI and the Alignment Workshops

Katja Grace co-founded AI Impacts, which runs the largest recurring surveys of what machine learning researchers expect from AI. She writes on forecasting, the case for slowing down AI and arguments for and against AI risk.
Runs the Expert Survey on Progress in AI (2,700+ researchers in 2023)
Essay 'Let's think about slowing down AI'
Long-running research on AI forecasting and discontinuities
Spencer Greenberg is a mathematician and entrepreneur who founded ClearerThinking.org and hosts the Clearer Thinking podcast.
Founder of ClearerThinking.org and Spark Wave
Host of the Clearer Thinking podcast
Conversations on rationality and AI risk
Ryan Greenblatt is chief scientist at Redwood Research. He was lead author of the 2024 'Alignment faking in large language models' paper and co-developed AI control.
Lead author of 'Alignment faking in large language models'
Detailed AI takeover and timelines analysis

Dylan Hadfield-Menell is an MIT professor who works on value alignment, from the theory of human–AI cooperation to how real AI systems fail. With Stuart Russell he co-authored the 'off-switch game' and 'cooperative inverse reinforcement learning' papers that formalised why uncertain AI defers to people.
Co-author of Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning and The Off-Switch Game
Work on Goodhart's law, incomplete specifications and overoptimization
Yuval Noah Harari is a historian and author of "Sapiens" and "Nexus". He warns that AI could concentrate power and undermine democracy and human agency.
Public debates on AI with Mustafa Suleyman and others
Signatory of calls to pause giant AI experiments

Jeremie Harris is co-founder and CEO of Gladstone AI, which wrote a 2024 US State Department-commissioned report on catastrophic AI risk. He earlier hosted the Towards Data Science podcast, interviewing many alignment researchers.
Co-author of the Gladstone AI action plan on AI national security risks (2024)
Hosted the Towards Data Science podcast
Co-hosts the Last Week in AI podcast
Tristan Harris is a former Google design ethicist and co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology. Known for 'The Social Dilemma', he now campaigns on the risks of the race to deploy powerful AI.
Co-created 'The AI Dilemma' talk with Aza Raskin (2023)
Featured in the Netflix documentary 'The Social Dilemma'

Demis Hassabis is co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for AlphaFold. He has repeatedly called for international cooperation and scientific caution as AI approaches AGI.
Co-founded DeepMind; led AlphaGo and AlphaFold
2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with John Jumper)
Signed the 2023 CAIS statement on extinction risk; calls for international AI safety standards

Lennart Heim is a researcher on compute governance, studying how control over AI chips and data centres can be used to govern frontier AI. He worked at the Centre for the Governance of AI before moving to RAND.
Leading voice on 'compute governance' – using chips as a lever for AI policy
Research on export controls and the US–China AI chip race
Co-authored work on compute thresholds and reporting requirements for frontier models
Dan Hendrycks directs the Center for AI Safety and advises xAI and Scale AI. He created the MMLU benchmark and GELU activation, and organised the 2023 statement on AI extinction risk.
Jacob Hilton leads the Alignment Research Center's theory work on heuristic explanations and low probability estimation. He previously worked at OpenAI on RLHF and WebGPT.
Earlier RLHF and WebGPT work at OpenAI

Geoffrey Hinton pioneered the neural-network methods behind modern AI, including backpropagation and Boltzmann machines, and won the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. In 2023 he left Google so he could speak freely about the risk that AI becomes smarter than us and takes control.
Co-inventor of key deep learning methods; Nobel Prize in Physics 2024
Left Google in 2023 to warn about AI risks
Argues digital intelligence may surpass and outcompete biological intelligence
Eric Ho is co-founder and CEO of Goodfire, which builds tools to understand and edit the internals of neural networks. He previously founded the recruiting startup RippleMatch.
Public advocacy for understanding AI internals
Marius Hobbhahn co-founded and leads Apollo Research, which studies scheming and deception in AI models. Apollo tests frontier models before release, and he testified to the US Senate in 2026.
Scheming and deception evaluations of frontier models
Jesse Hoogland co-founded Timaeus (now Resolution), which applies singular learning theory to understand how neural networks develop. His work pioneered developmental interpretability.
Applying singular learning theory to safety
George Hotz is a hacker and entrepreneur who founded comma.ai and tiny corp. In AI safety he appears mainly as a sceptical debater, arguing against fast AI takeover scenarios.
First to jailbreak the iPhone; founder of comma.ai (self-driving) and tiny corp
Public debates with Eliezer Yudkowsky and Connor Leahy on AI risk
Evan Hubinger leads Alignment Stress-Testing at Anthropic, building 'model organisms' of misalignment. He is lead author of 'Risks from Learned Optimization' and of the Sleeper Agents paper.
Introduced inner alignment and mesa-optimization ('Risks from Learned Optimization')
Sleeper Agents: deceptive behaviour that survives safety training
Model organisms work including alignment faking and reward-hacking misalignment
Director, AI: Futures and Responsibility programme

Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh is a Cambridge researcher who was the founding executive director of the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk. He works on AI governance, international cooperation and US–China relations on AI safety.
Co-founded the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence
Research on West–China cooperation on AI safety and AI race narratives
Axel Højmark is a researcher at Apollo Research, which evaluates AI systems for scheming and deception. He discusses how Apollo tests models for hidden goals.
Evaluations for scheming at Apollo Research
Discussed testing AI for hidden goals on Machine Learning Street Talk

Geoffrey Irving is a veteran safety researcher who led safety teams at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and was chief scientist of the UK AI Security Institute. He is best known for proposing AI safety via debate.
Chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute
Puts the odds of a good AI outcome near a coin flip
Jared Kaplan is a co-founder and Chief Science Officer of Anthropic and a former Johns Hopkins theoretical physicist. He led the 2020 work on neural scaling laws.
Neural scaling laws for language models
Co-developed Constitutional AI and Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy
Public forecasts of human-level AI around 2027–2030
Member of technical staff (formerly co-CEO of Open Philanthropy)

Holden Karnofsky co-founded GiveWell and Open Philanthropy, which became one of the largest funders of AI safety work. His 'Most Important Century' blog series argued that transformative AI could make this century pivotal, and he now works on safety strategy at Anthropic.
Co-founder of GiveWell and Open Philanthropy
'Most Important Century' series on Cold Takes
Ideas like if-then commitments for AI risk reduction

Akbir Khan is an AI safety researcher who works on scalable oversight. He was lead author of a 2024 ICML best-paper study showing that debating with more persuasive AI models helps humans reach truer answers.
Lead author of "Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers" (ICML 2024 best paper)
Research on debate as a scalable oversight method
PhD work at University College London
